value.overview: The Rusty-margined Flycatcher (Myiozetetes cayanensis) is a small tropical tyrant flycatcher found from Central America through much of northern and central South America. It is named for the rusty or rufous edges visible on its wings and tail. This active bird often perches conspicuously on exposed branches, then sallies out to catch insects. It also eats small fruits and is commonly associated with forest edges, riversides, gardens, plantations, and other partly open habitats.
value.classification: The Rusty-margined Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Myiozetetes. It is closely related to other medium-sized, strongly patterned flycatchers of tropical America.
value.identification: This flycatcher has olive-brown upperparts, yellow underparts, a dark mask through the eye, and a contrasting pale or whitish eyebrow. The wings and tail show noticeable rusty or rufous edging, especially when the bird moves or spreads its wings. Its bill is dark, and the body is compact with a fairly upright posture. It can resemble the Social Flycatcher and other Myiozetetes species, but the rusty wing margins and facial pattern are useful identification features.
value.rangeHabitat: The Rusty-margined Flycatcher ranges from Costa Rica and Panama south through northern and central South America, including the Amazon Basin and parts of the Atlantic Forest region. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in lowland and foothill areas, particularly in warm humid regions and along forest edges, river corridors, second growth, farmland, plantations, and gardens. It generally avoids dense interior forest and often benefits from a mosaic of woodland and open vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable lowland and foothill habitats, although local movements may occur in response to food availability, rainfall, or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: The species usually breeds during the wetter or locally favorable part of the year, with timing varying across its broad range. It builds a bulky enclosed or partially enclosed nest from plant fibers and other materials, commonly placed in a tree, shrub, or human-made structure. The nest may have a side entrance or protected opening. Both adults participate in territorial defense and care for the young, and the species may nest near other flycatchers or around disturbed habitats.
value.dietFeeding: Rusty-margined Flycatchers feed mainly on insects and other arthropods captured during short flights from an exposed perch. They may also take prey from vegetation or the ground and sometimes eat small fruits and berries. Their feeding style is active and conspicuous: the bird watches from a branch, makes a quick sally to seize prey, and returns to a perch or nearby cover.
value.behavior: This species is usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small family groups. It frequently perches in open positions and gives sharp calls while defending a feeding or nesting area. Rusty-margined Flycatchers are alert and energetic, often flicking the wings or tail and making repeated short flights. They may join mixed-species feeding flocks, especially along forest edges, but can also be conspicuous around gardens, roadsides, and clearings.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and is not considered globally threatened; a precise population trend is not well established.
